title: Installation fails on Windows ARM64 (aarch64) due to yaml12 Rust compilation target error
description:
### Description
Hi! When trying to install `Rapp` (v0.4.0) on a Windows ARM64 system (aarch64), the installation fails during the compilation of the new dependency `yaml12`. 

The `yaml12` build script (`Makevars.win`) likely forces Cargo to compile for a GNU target, but it drops the architecture prefix, resulting in `--target -pc-windows-gnu` instead of `aarch64-pc-windows-gnu`. Furthermore, the official stable Rust toolchain for Windows ARM64 (`stable-aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`) does not inherently support the GNU target, if I understand it correctly.

### Standard Output / Error Message
During `devtools::install()` or `pak::pak()`, the build fails with the following Cargo error:

```
RUSTFLAGS=" --print=native-static-libs" cargo build -j 2 --offline --target=-pc-windows-gnu --lib --release --manifest-path=rust/Cargo.toml --target-dir=./rust/target
error: failed to run `rustc` to learn about target-specific information

Caused by:
  process didn't exit successfully: `...\bin\rustc.exe - --crate-name ___ --print=file-names --print=native-static-libs --target -pc-windows-gnu ...` (exit code: 1)
  --- stderr
  error: error loading target specification: could not find specification for target "-pc-windows-gnu"
```

### Environment
- **OS:** Windows 11 (ARM64 / aarch64)
- **R Version:** 4.5.x (aarch64-w64-mingw32)
- **Rust Toolchain:** stable-aarch64-pc-windows-msvc
- **Rapp Version:** 0.4.0 (relies on `yaml12` v0.1.0)

### Suggested Fix / Workaround
For now, rolling back to `Rapp` v0.3.0 bypasses the issue since it doesn't depend on `yaml12`. 
For v0.4.0+, the configuration script in `yaml12` needs, if possible, to properly detect the `aarch64` architecture on Windows when setting up the `--target` flag for Cargo, or fallback gracefully if the required target isn't supported by the host's MSVC toolchain.

title: feature: allow positional arguments' help to render before options
description:
Positional args show in the usage line (<PATH>) but their description renders last, after Options and Global options

i feel like this buries the most important input below less critical flags

<details>
<summary>Rapp Script</summary>

	```r
	#!/usr/bin/env Rapp
	#| name: example
	#| description: Minimal repro — positional args render below options in help.
	
	#| description: Server URL
	url <- "https://example.com"
	
	#| description: Auth token
	token <- NA_character_
	
	switch(
	  command <- "",
	
	  upload = {
	    #| description: File to upload
	    #| arg-type: positional
	    path <- NULL
	
	    #| description: Target name
	    target <- "default"
	
	    #| description: Replace existing file
	    replace <- FALSE
	
	    cat("Uploading", path, "to", target, "\n")
	  }
	)
	```

</details>

```console
➜ Rapp /tmp/rapp-issue-repro.R upload --help
Usage: example upload [OPTIONS] <PATH>

upload command

Options:
  --target <TARGET>         Target name [default: "default"] [type: string]
  --replace / --no-replace  Replace existing file [default: false]
                            Enable with `--replace`.

Global options:
  --url <URL>      Server URL [default: "https://example.com"] [type: string]
  --token <TOKEN>  Auth token [default: "NA"] [type: string]

Arguments:
  <PATH>  File to upload
```
Especially in my case, where we have lots of options + some global options, the position args really get buried,

I would expect more like:

```console
Usage: example upload [OPTIONS] <PATH>

upload command

Arguments:
  <PATH>  File to upload

Options:
  --target <TARGET>         Target name [default: "default"] [type: string]
  --replace / --no-replace  Replace existing file [default: false]
                            Enable with `--replace`.
Global options:
  --url <URL>      Server URL [default: "https://example.com"] [type: string]
  --token <TOKEN>  Auth token [default: "NA"] [type: string]
```

## Python equivalent default


```python
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Minimal example.")
parser.add_argument("--url", default="https://example.com", help="Server URL")
parser.add_argument("--token", default=None, help="Auth token")

sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")
upload = sub.add_parser("upload", help="Upload a file")
upload.add_argument("path", help="File to upload")
upload.add_argument("--target", default="default", help="Target name")
upload.add_argument("--replace", action="store_true", help="Replace existing file")

args = parser.parse_args()
```

```console
python3 /tmp/example_cli.py upload --help 2>&1
usage: example_cli.py upload [-h] [--target TARGET] [--replace] path

positional arguments:
  path             File to upload

options:
  -h, --help       show this help message and exit
  --target TARGET  Target name
  --replace        Replace existing file

```

title: Disabling automatic creation of `--no-*` flag for boolean flags
description:
Is it possible to disable the creation of the `--no-*` flags for boolean value flags? Sometimes, in cases like `--version`, you may not want the explicit false option.

```
❯ _dev/reprex-cli-boolean-flag.R --help
Usage: my-app [OPTIONS]

A simple example CLI app.

Options:
  --version / --no-version  Print version and exit. [default: false]
                            Enable with `--version`.
```

```r
#!/usr/bin/env Rapp
#| name: my-app
#| description: A simple example CLI app.

#| description: Print version and exit.
version <- FALSE

if (version) {
  cat("my-app 1.0.0\n")
  quit(status = 0)
}

cat("Hello, world!\n")
```

title: Show help when subcommand is omitted; expose programmatic help API
description:
## Problem

When using `switch(command <- "", ...)` for subcommands, running the app without a subcommand causes the switch to silently fall through — no output, no guidance. Using `switch(command <- NULL, ...)` instead makes the subcommand required, but the error message isn't helpful ("EXPR must be a length 1 vector"). Neither outcome matches what users expect from a CLI tool.

Most CLI tools (e.g., `git`, `cargo`, `gh`) print help text when invoked without a required subcommand. Rapp already generates excellent help output via `--help`, but there's no way to trigger that behavior automatically or programmatically from within a script.

## Current workaround

It's possible to call `Rapp:::print_app_help()` with `commandArgs(TRUE)[1]` to recover the script path and print scoped help after each switch:

```r
show_help <- function(...) {
  script_path <- commandArgs(TRUE)[1]
  Rapp:::print_app_help(script_path, yaml = FALSE, command_path = c(...))
  quit(status = 1)
}

switch(
  command <- "",
  list = { ... },
  add = { ... }
)
if (command == "") show_help()
```

This has two problems:
- It relies on an internal function and `commandArgs(TRUE)[1]` happening to contain the script path, which breaks under `Rapp::run()` in tests.
- It requires boilerplate after every switch at every nesting level.

## Proposal

### 1. Auto-help when no subcommand is given

When a `switch()` receives no subcommand (i.e., the default `""` is used and no branch matches), Rapp could automatically print the scoped help for that command level and exit — the same as if `--help` had been passed at that position.

This would make `myapp`, `myapp list`, and `myapp list --help` all produce the appropriate help output without any user code.

If this is too opinionated as a default, it could be opt-in via annotation, e.g.:

```r
#| help-on-missing-command: true
switch(command <- "", ...)
```

### 2. Programmatic help API

A public function to print help from within a running script, e.g.:

```r
Rapp::print_help()          # top-level help
Rapp::print_help("list")    # scoped to "list" subcommand
```

This would let scripts handle the missing-subcommand case themselves while producing the same output as `--help`. It would work correctly under `Rapp::run()` in tests since Rapp already has the app context at that point.

title: Control automatic coercion of arguments to the expected type
description:
Hi @t-kalinowski,

I am enjoying playing around with this package. Thanks for your work on it!

I noticed that, by default, `Rapp` coerces arguments to the expected type, at least if the type is type-adjacent (i.e, coercible). For example, in your `flip-coin` example, if you provide a numeric with decimals (not interger-ish), it is coerced automatically to an integer. This seems like a nice QoL coercion, but it also means the program can't catch this bad argument and communicate it to the user.

The help docs indicate it needs to be an integer, but the user can pass decimal values or even logicals, as shown below, and coercion means the issue isn't flagged. Coercion for characters seems to fail silently, so then the error is thrown. Do you think this is the desired behaviour?

```r
#!/usr/bin/env Rapp
#| name: flip-coin
#| description: |
#|   Flip a coin.

#| description: Number of coin flips
#| short: 'n'
flips <- 1L

if (!rlang::is_integerish(flips)) {
  rlang::abort("Not an integer!")
}

cat(flips)
```
``` r
Rapp::run("foo.R", c("--help"))
#> Usage: flip-coin [OPTIONS]
#> 
#> Flip a coin.
#> 
#> Options:
#>   -n, --flips <FLIPS>  Number of coin flips [default: 1] [type: integer]

Rapp::run("foo.R", c("-n", 10.2))
#> 10

Rapp::run("foo.R", c("-n", TRUE))
#> 1

Rapp::run("foo.R", c("-n", "Hello"))
#> Hello
#> Error:
#> ! Not an integer!
```

title: #| example: annotation support for subcommands (LLM/agent-friendly CLIs)
description:
## Feature request

Add support for an `#| example:` annotation that attaches usage examples to commands and options, displayed in `--help` output.

```r
switch("",
  #| title: Parliamentary bills
  #| description: Search bills from Camera or Senato.
  #| example: italyparl bills --approved --camera cd
  #| example: italyparl bills --keyword energia --camera sn --format jsonlines
  bills = {
    ...
  }
)
```

Expected `--help` output:

```
bills:
  Search bills from Camera or Senato.

  Options:
    --camera     cd or sn [default: "cd"]
    --keyword    Keyword to search in title [default: ""]
    --approved   Only approved bills [default: false]

  Examples:
    italyparl bills --approved --camera cd
    italyparl bills --keyword energia --camera sn --format jsonlines
```

## Why this matters: LLM-orchestrated CLIs

CLIs are increasingly used by LLM agents (Claude, GPT, etc.) as tools in agentic workflows. When an agent discovers a CLI, it runs `--help` to understand how to use it. Examples in `--help` are the single most effective signal for an agent: it pattern-matches off a concrete invocation far faster and more reliably than it parses a prose description.

Without native example support, the only workaround is a hand-written `examples` subcommand — which works but is redundant and decoupled from the commands it documents.

Adding `#| example:` would make Rapp CLIs first-class tools for agent use with zero extra code from the CLI author.

title: Simplify script installation
description:
I quite like this package and approach. Thus, I would like to include a lesson I recently learnt while developing an R code aims to include some CLI tools. It is possible to include the following line in the `R/configure` file:

```R
#!/bin/bash

# Determine the user's shell configuration file
SHELL_RC="$(basename $SHELL)rc"
USER_RC="$HOME/.$SHELL_RC"

# Define color codes
GREEN='\033[0;32m'
YELLOW='\033[1;33m'
NC='\033[0m'


# Add the exec directory of the package to the PATH
export PATH=$(Rscript -e "cat(system.file(\"exec\", package = \"yourpackagename\"))"):$PATH
EXPORT_CMD='export PATH=$(Rscript -e "cat(system.file(\"exec\", package = \"yourpackagename\"))"):$PATH'
if ! grep -Fxq "$EXPORT_CMD" "$USER_RC"; then
    echo "$EXPORT_CMD" >> "$USER_RC"
    echo -e "${GREEN}Added yourpackagename exec directory to PATH in $USER_RC${NC}"
else
    echo -e "${YELLOW}yourpackagename exec directory already in PATH in $USER_RC${NC}"
fi
echo -e "${YELLOW}Please run 'source $USER_RC' before using the command.${NC}"
# Source the user's shell configuration file to apply changes
source "$USER_RC"

```

This way it is not necessary to communicate with users to include the proper export in their `.bashrc` or `./zshrc` as it will be automatically identified.
